Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

very adverb

before adjectives and adverbs

also extremely, really, not particularly, highly (highly likely)

classical

Cic. Fam. 15.17.3: exspectātiō valdē magna (Lewis & Short)
Petr. 31.3: gustātiō valdē lauta
Traupman 401

valdē

adverb

very, very much

With adjectives, adverbs and verbs. Latin’s commonest “very”, though, is no separate word: the superlative (facillimē, very easily: Cic. Fam. 9.24.3) or per- on the adjective or adverb (perbellē, very nicely: Cic. Att. 4.4a.1).

Other words

  • admodum — very, quite

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 3.36: admodum paucī (Lewis & Short); Cic. Sen. 10: nōn admodum grandem nātū (Lewis & Short); Traupman 401

    Often after its word (paucī admodum); nōn admodum, not very.

  • perquam — extremely, as … as can be

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 2.201: perquam breviter (Lewis & Short); Plin. Ep. 7.27.1: perquam velim scīre (Lewis & Short)

  • oppidō — very, utterly

    adverb · also used · classical · Plaut. Am. 1.1.143: oppidō interiī (Lewis & Short); Cic. Fam. 14.4.4: oppidō paucī (Lewis & Short)

    (vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.; Cic. in epistulīs)

    Lewis & Short: confined to familiar talk, and already old-fashioned in Quintilian’s day (Quint. 8.3.25).

Examples

  • valdē aveō scīre quid agās

    I very much want to know how you areCic. Att. 1.15.2

  • allāta est tamen gustātiō valdē lauta

    still, the starters that were brought in were very grandPetr. 31.3

  • Corcȳram bellissimē nāvigāvimus

    we had a very pleasant crossing to CorcyraCic. Fam. 16.9.1

See also a lot, tiny, very early, far.
